steps.title: What film music does
steps.body:
**Music for stage and screen** is music written to serve a story. That changes the questions you ask about it: not just *what is happening in the music*, but *what is it doing for the film?*

Two terms come first.

**Non-diegetic** music is the score: heard by the audience, not by the characters. The *Star Wars* main title is non-diegetic. **Diegetic** music belongs inside the story — a radio playing, a band on screen, like the cantina band later in the same film.

Then what film music is *for*: setting a mood, telling you how to feel about a character, building tension, marking the scale of an event, and joining scenes together. Every device in this set work is doing one of those jobs, and saying which job is where the marks are.

visuals.alt: A table of the jobs film music does, with an example of each from Star Wars

check.prompt: The main title plays while words scroll up the screen. The characters cannot hear it. What kind of music is it?
check.solution: Music the characters cannot hear is **non-diegetic**: the score, for the audience only.

steps.title: Star Wars: the facts to know cold
steps.body:
Composed by **John Williams** for the film *Star Wars* (**1977**), later retitled *Episode IV: A New Hope*, directed by George Lucas. The score was recorded by the **London Symphony Orchestra**. It is one of the two **music for stage and screen** set works, with *Defying Gravity* from *Wicked*.

The set work is the **main title** leading into the **Rebel Blockade Runner**: the music heard as the opening words scroll up the screen, followed by the chase that begins the film.

The context examiners like: in the late 1960s and 1970s many films had turned to pop and rock scores. Williams went back to the **full symphonic, late-Romantic sound** of Golden Age Hollywood composers such as **Korngold**, and to **Wagner's** idea of the **leitmotif**. A huge orchestra, big themes, themes with jobs.

visuals.alt: A table of the key facts about the Star Wars main title

check.solution: The **London Symphony Orchestra** recorded it, one reason it sounds like a concert work rather than a film soundtrack of its time.

steps.title: Leitmotif: a theme with a job
steps.body:
A **leitmotif** is a short musical idea tied to a character, a place or an idea. Wagner built whole operas out of them; Williams built a film series.

The main theme is **Luke Skywalker's** leitmotif. Once the audience links the tune with the character, the composer can bring it back whenever the story turns to him — and change it to say something new. The same theme played slowly and quietly by a single horn means something very different from the full brass at the start.

That is why a leitmotif is powerful: it lets music **signal a character or idea even when they are not on screen**, and **comment** on what is happening to them.

In an exam, *leitmotif* is the term, *Wagner* is the origin, and *it can return changed* is the point.

steps.text: Full brass, fortissimo, fast: *the hero, triumphant*
Solo horn, quiet, slow: *the hero, alone or remembering*
Minor key, low strings: *the hero, in danger or defeat*
The notes barely change; the timbre, dynamics, tempo and key do
steps.note: That flexibility is what makes a leitmotif useful

check.prompt: Luke Skywalker's main theme returns whenever the story turns to him. What is it an example of?
check.solution: A theme tied to a character and brought back when he matters is a **leitmotif**.

steps.title: The structure, section by section
steps.body:
The set work runs in seven parts. Learn them in order, then hear them in order.

The main title has an **AABA** shape at its heart — the main theme **A** stated twice, a contrasting **B**, then **A** again — framed by a loud opening and followed by a transition into the action music.

There are no timings here on purpose. Recordings differ, and a map you make yourself while listening is worth far more than one you read. The your-turn step asks you to make it.

rows: one loud chord from the whole orchestra, then brass fanfare
trumpets, heroic: triplet pick-up, leap up a fifth
the theme again, still in the trumpets
softer and more lyrical, strings and woodwind
sudden drop to quiet, mysterious and uncertain
action: fast, dissonant, driven by repeated rhythms
props.title: Main title into Rebel Blockade Runner

visuals.alt: A table of the six sections of the Star Wars main title and Rebel Blockade Runner, in order, with what to listen for in each

check.prompt: What comes straight after the contrasting B theme?
check.solution: After the contrast, the **main theme returns**: A A B A. Only then comes the quiet transition and the action music.

steps.title: How the main theme sounds heroic
steps.body:
A *how* question wants devices tied to their effect. For the main theme there are four, one per element.

**Timbre.** The brass, led by trumpets — for centuries the sound of ceremony and heroism.

**Melody.** A **triplet pick-up**, three quick notes, throws the tune forward onto the strong beat, then it **leaps up a perfect fifth**, B flat to F. A wide, open rising leap sounds bold; a small step would not.

**Harmony and tonality.** Clearly **B flat major**, so the tonality never sounds in doubt — but the harmony is not plain. Pearson's guide points out that in the opening bars almost half the chords are **quartal**, built from fourths rather than thirds, and there are few conventional cadences. Certain tonality, unusual harmony: that is part of why it sounds grand rather than ordinary.

**Dynamics and texture.** A **fortissimo tutti** chord — the whole orchestra — then the theme **doubled in octaves** across the orchestra, so it sounds enormous.

And underneath it all, a **march-like 4/4**.

visuals.alt: Four boxes showing how timbre, melody, harmony, and dynamics and texture each make the main theme sound heroic

visuals.problem: Turning a device into an answer

steps.text: *It uses brass.* — names a timbre, no effect
*The theme leaps up a perfect fifth.* — a device, still no effect
steps.note: A list of features is not an explanation

steps.text: *The theme leaps up a perfect fifth after a triplet pick-up, a wide, open interval that sounds bold and confident.*
steps.note: Device plus effect: that is what the mark is for

check.solution: Only the first names devices and ties them to an effect. The others are fame, a bare fact and repetition of *exciting*.
options: The theme leaps up a fifth after a quick pick-up, which sounds bold and confident
The theme is extremely famous and everyone recognises it straight away
The theme is played by the brass section of the orchestra at the start
The theme is very exciting and makes the listener feel really excited

steps.title: The Rebel Blockade Runner: music for a chase
steps.body:
After a sudden drop to a **quiet, uncertain** transition, the action music bursts in. On screen, a small rebel ship is being chased and fired on by an enormous Imperial ship, and the music is built for exactly that.

- **Faster tempo**, for the speed of the chase.
- **Repeated rhythmic patterns** — an **ostinato** — that keep driving without a break, so the pursuit feels relentless.
- Far more **dissonance** than the main theme, so it sounds dangerous.
- **Brass stabs** and **percussion**, landing like impacts.

The contrast with the main theme is the whole point: one presents a **character**, the other depicts an **event**.

rows: B flat major, some quartal chords
props.title: The same orchestra, opposite jobs

visuals.alt: A table contrasting the main theme with the Rebel Blockade Runner section element by element

check.prompt: Which device, a pattern repeated over and over, drives the action music?
check.solution: A continuously repeated pattern is an **ostinato**. It keeps the chase moving without letting the tension drop.

steps.title: Your turn: make your own map
steps.body:
Play the soundtrack recording of the main title and Rebel Blockade Runner on whatever the family uses. On paper, copy the table below and write the time each section starts as you hear it arrive.

Then play it again and check. The second listen is where the learning happens: you will hear sections coming that you missed the first time.

What to catch, in order of difficulty:

1. The opening chord and the main theme — impossible to miss.
2. The softer B theme arriving.
3. The main theme's return.
4. The drop to the quiet transition.
5. The moment the action music bursts in.

props.title: Your map: fill in the times as you listen

visuals.alt: A blank listening map: the six sections in order with an empty column for the time each starts

steps.text: Recordings differ in speed and in what they include, so printed timings often do not line up
Listening for the next section is the skill Section A tests
A map you made is one you remember

check.solution: Opening chord, main theme **A**, contrasting **B**, **A** again, the quiet transition, then the Rebel Blockade Runner.

opening, B, A, transition, A, action

steps.title: Grade 9: effects, not features, and comparing sections
steps.body:
The grade 9 habits here are the same as for every set work, applied to film.

**Tie every device to what it does for the film.** *The brass plays the theme* is a feature. *The brass, the sound of ceremony, tells you this is a hero before you see him* is an answer. The film is the reason every device is there; say which job each one does.

**Compare by element.** A question on the main theme and the action music is a comparison, and it is marked as one. Melody in both, then harmony in both, then rhythm, then texture — never a paragraph on each section in turn.

**Finish with a judgement.** Not *they are different*, but what the difference achieves: the main theme presents a character, stable and heroic; the action music depicts an event, unstable and threatened. That sentence is what reaches level 4.

**Use the context properly.** *1977* and *Korngold* earn marks only when they explain something audible: the full late-Romantic orchestra is the revival of Golden Age Hollywood, at a time when many films used pop scores.

rows: the brass, the sound of ceremony, marks a hero
a rising fifth sounds open and confident
dissonance and ostinato make the chase relentless
a character presented, an event depicted
props.title: Effects, not features

visuals.alt: A table pairing a weak answer with a grade 9 answer for this set work

check.prompt: Which sentence belongs in a level 4 comparison of the two sections?
check.solution: The first compares both sections on one element, harmony, and says what the difference does. The others are context, a losing structure, and a claim with no detail.
options: Where the theme's B flat major sounds certain, the chase's dissonance sounds threatened
The main theme was written by John Williams in 1977 for Star Wars
I will write about the main theme first and the chase music second
The action music is louder and has more instruments playing in it

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- **The set work**: John Williams, *Star Wars*, **1977**, recorded by the **London Symphony Orchestra**. Area of study: **music for stage and screen**.
- **Non-diegetic**: the score, heard by the audience not the characters. **Diegetic**: music inside the story.
- **Leitmotif** (Wagner's technique): the main theme is Luke Skywalker's, and it can return changed to comment on him.
- **Structure**: opening tutti chord and fanfare → main theme **A** twice → contrasting **B** → **A** returns → quiet transition → **Rebel Blockade Runner**. An AABA shape at its heart.
- **Heroic main theme**: brass timbre, triplet pick-up, rising **perfect fifth**, clear **B flat major** tonality with some **quartal** chords, fortissimo tutti, octave doubling, march-like **4/4**.
- **Action music**: faster, dissonant, driven by **ostinato**, brass stabs and percussion.
- **Context**: a revival of the late-Romantic Golden Age Hollywood sound (Korngold), when many films used pop scores.
- **Answers**: device plus the job it does for the film; comparisons by element; finish with a judgement.
- **Make your own listening map** — printed timings rarely match your recording.

visuals.alt: A summary table of the Star Wars main title by element with the term to use

questions.prompt: In which area of study is the *Star Wars* main title?
questions.solution: It is one of the two **music for stage and screen** set works, with *Defying Gravity* from *Wicked*. Section B can set it against an unfamiliar film or stage extract.

questions.prompt: Name the composer of the *Star Wars* main title.
questions.solution: **John Williams**, who also scored *Jaws*, *E.T.* and the *Harry Potter* films. George Lucas directed the film.

questions.prompt: In which year was the first *Star Wars* film released?
questions.solution: **1977.** It was later retitled *Episode IV: A New Hope*.

questions.prompt: Which section of the orchestra plays the main theme at the start?
questions.solution: The **brass**, led by the trumpets. Brass is the traditional sound of heroism and ceremony, which is exactly what the opening wants.

questions.prompt: Name the term for a short recurring musical idea linked to a character, place or idea.
questions.solution: A **leitmotif**, a technique Wagner developed in his operas. The main theme is Luke Skywalker's leitmotif, so it can return whenever the story turns to him.

questions.prompt: In which key does the main title open?
questions.solution: **B flat major**, a bright, open key for brass. The whole of the opening is major and triadic, which is part of why it sounds confident.

questions.prompt: Give the time signature of the main theme.
questions.solution: **4/4**, four crotchet beats in a bar. With its strong beats and dotted and triplet rhythms, it gives the theme the character of a march.

questions.prompt: The main theme leaps up from its first long note. Which interval is it?
questions.solution: A **perfect fifth**, B flat up to F. Counting letter names, B–C–D–E–F is five, so it is a fifth. A wide, open rising leap is a classic way to sound bold and heroic.

questions.prompt: Name the term for music in a film that the characters themselves cannot hear.
questions.solution: **Non-diegetic** music, the score, is heard by the audience but not by the characters. **Diegetic** music belongs to the world of the story, such as the band playing in the *Star Wars* cantina.

questions.prompt: How does the Rebel Blockade Runner section differ from the main theme?
questions.solution: The action music is **faster**, **more dissonant** and built on **repeated rhythmic patterns**, because it accompanies a chase. The main theme is steady, consonant and melodic.

markScheme.description: faster, more dissonant, driven by repeated rhythms

options: It is faster, more dissonant and driven by repeated rhythms
It is slower and lyrical, played by a solo cello
It is quieter, in a minor key, for a solo voice
It is unaccompanied and in a free, unmeasured rhythm

questions.prompt: Explain how Williams makes the main theme sound heroic.
questions.solution: Named devices, each tied to its effect. **Timbre**: brass, led by trumpets, the sound of ceremony. **Melody**: a triplet pick-up drives onto a rising perfect fifth, a wide, open, confident leap. **Tonality and harmony**: clearly B flat major, so the tonality sounds certain, even though some of the chords are quartal. **Dynamics and texture**: a fortissimo tutti chord, and the theme doubled in octaves, so it sounds enormous. **Rhythm**: a march-like 4/4.

markScheme.description: Level 1 (1 to 2): devices named with little or no effect given
Level 2 (3 to 4): some devices linked to their effect, with limited reference to the music
Level 3 (5 to 6): devices named, each tied to its effect and located in the music

criteria.text: Brass timbre named, with its association with heroism or ceremony
The triplet pick-up and rising perfect fifth, tied to a bold, confident sound
The clear B flat major tonality, tied to a sense of certainty
Fortissimo, tutti or octave doubling, tied to the sense of scale

questions.modelAnswer: Williams gives the theme to the **brass**, led by the trumpets, whose timbre has long been the sound of ceremony and heroism, so the listener hears a hero before seeing one. The melody opens with a **triplet pick-up** that drives forward onto the strong beat and then **leaps up a perfect fifth**; a wide, open rising interval sounds bold and confident in a way a small step cannot. It is firmly in **B flat major**, so the tonality never sounds in doubt, even though some of the chords are built in fourths rather than plain triads. The first chord is a **fortissimo tutti**, the whole orchestra at once, and the theme is **doubled in octaves** across the orchestra, which gives it an enormous scale. The steady **4/4** with dotted and triplet rhythms makes it march, and marching is what heroes do.

questions.prompt: Why does the quick triplet at the start of the theme give it energy?
questions.solution: An **anacrusis** (pick-up) of quick notes throws the music forward onto the downbeat, like a run-up before a jump. It does not slow the tempo, change key or thin the texture.

markScheme.description: it drives forward onto the strong first beat

options: The quick notes drive forward onto the strong first beat
The three notes slow the tempo down before the theme
The triplet changes the key briefly to the minor
The triplet removes the accompaniment for a moment

questions.prompt: Name the film-music technique in which the music closely mirrors specific movements on screen.
questions.solution: **Mickey-mousing**, named after cartoons in which the music copies every movement. It is a term to have ready for unfamiliar film extracts in Section B, where it may fit better than it does here.

questions.prompt: In a comparison of the main theme with the Rebel Blockade Runner section, which sentence scores highest?
questions.solution: Only the first compares both sections on one element, harmony, in the same sentence, and says what the difference does. The others describe one side, announce a structure that loses marks, or say nothing technical.
options: Where the main theme is clearly in B flat major, the action music is dissonant, so tension replaces confidence
The main theme is played by the brass and is very famous from the films and the trailers
First I will describe the main theme, and then I will describe the Rebel Blockade Runner
Both of the sections are exciting and both are played by a very large symphony orchestra

questions.prompt: Why is a leitmotif useful to a film composer?
questions.solution: Because the audience learns to link the theme with the character, the composer can bring it back — changed in instrument, speed or key — to remind, foreshadow or comment, even when that character is absent.

markScheme.description: it signals a character or idea even when they are absent

options: It lets the music signal a character or idea even when they are not on screen
It guarantees that every scene in the film uses exactly the same tempo
It means the orchestra does not need to follow the conductor at all
It allows the composer to avoid writing any new music for the sequel

questions.prompt: Why was Williams's score notable when it appeared in 1977?
questions.solution: Film music in the late 1960s and 1970s had often turned to pop and rock. Williams went back to the late-Romantic symphonic sound of Golden Age Hollywood composers such as Korngold, played by the London Symphony Orchestra. Orchestral film scores existed long before, and the score is full of recurring themes.

markScheme.description: it revived the full symphonic style

options: It revived the full symphonic style of classic Hollywood when many films used pop scores
It was the first score for any film ever recorded by a full symphony orchestra
It used only electronic synthesisers, with no acoustic instruments anywhere
It contained no recurring themes at all, which was new for a film of its size

questions.prompt: Compare the main theme with the Rebel Blockade Runner section. Refer to melody, harmony, rhythm and texture.
questions.solution: Organised by element, both sections in each paragraph, ending in a judgement. Melody: a memorable theme built on a leap against fragmented motifs. Harmony: a clear B flat major, with some quartal chords, against dissonant and unstable. Rhythm: a steady march with a triplet pick-up against fast repeated patterns. Texture: a melody over chords, doubled in octaves, against layered rhythmic figures and stabs. Judgement: the theme presents a character, the action music presents an event.

markScheme.description: Level 1 (1 to 3): separate descriptions with few technical terms and no real comparison
Level 2 (4 to 6): some comparison, loosely organised, with some correct terminology
Level 3 (7 to 9): comparison organised by element, accurate terms, evidence from both sections
Level 4 (10 to 12): sustained comparison by element, with a judgement about what the differences do

criteria.text: Melody compared: a memorable theme with a rising leap against short, fragmented motifs
Harmony compared: a clear B flat major against dissonant and unstable
Rhythm and texture compared: a steady march over chords against fast ostinato-like patterns and brass stabs
A judgement about what the differences do — a character presented against an event depicted

questions.modelAnswer: The two sections do opposite jobs, and every element shows it. In **melody**, the main theme is a long, singable tune that leaps up a perfect fifth after a triplet pick-up, made to be remembered, while the action music breaks into short fragments and motifs that are too restless to sing. In **harmony**, the theme sits clearly in B flat major, so it sounds certain even where its chords are built in fourths, whereas the Rebel Blockade Runner is dissonant and unstable, so it sounds threatened. In **rhythm**, the theme marches steadily in 4/4, while the action music is faster and driven by repeated patterns that never let the tension drop. In **texture**, the theme is a melody over chords, doubled in octaves for weight; the action music layers rhythmic figures and sharp brass stabs. Taken together, the main theme presents a *character* — confident, heroic, stable — and the action music depicts an *event*, a chase in progress, which is why nothing in it settles.

questions.prompt: Explain how the music of the Rebel Blockade Runner section suits the on-screen chase.
questions.solution: Devices tied to the chase. Faster tempo for speed; repeated rhythmic patterns for relentless pursuit; dissonance for danger; brass stabs and percussion for impacts and gunfire; a sudden contrast with the quiet transition so the action bursts in.

markScheme.description: Level 1 (1 to 2): devices named with little or no effect given
Level 2 (3 to 4): some devices linked to their effect, with limited reference to the music
Level 3 (5 to 6): devices named, each tied to its effect and located in the music

criteria.text: Tempo and repeated rhythms tied to speed and relentless pursuit
Dissonance tied to danger or threat
Brass stabs, percussion or the contrast with the quiet transition, tied to impact

questions.modelAnswer: The section accompanies a small rebel ship being chased and fired on by a vast Imperial ship. The **faster tempo** matches the speed of the chase, and **repeated rhythmic patterns** keep driving forward without a break, which makes the pursuit feel relentless. **Dissonant** harmony replaces the plain triads of the main theme, so the music sounds dangerous rather than heroic. **Sharp brass stabs** and **percussion** land like impacts and gunfire. And because it bursts in straight after the **quiet, uncertain transition**, the contrast in dynamics and texture makes the attack feel sudden, which is exactly how it appears on screen.

examTechnique.body:
Film music is marked like every set work, with one extra question to ask of every device: what is it doing for the film? A *how* question on this set work wants the device, the effect, and the job that effect does — announcing a hero, building tension, depicting a chase.

Section A questions are short and precise: one term for one mark, correctly spelled. Know the facts cold — Williams, 1977, the London Symphony Orchestra, B flat major, 4/4 — so no time goes on recalling them. Section B may set this piece against an unfamiliar film or stage extract from the same area of study; compare by element, both pieces in every paragraph, and end with a judgement.

And listen. Play the soundtrack recording and make your own map of the six sections. Section A plays the extract, so the structure has to be recognisable by ear.
examinerErrors: Listing features with no effect: *the brass plays the theme*. The mark is for what it does — the sound of ceremony, announcing a hero.
Confusing diegetic and non-diegetic. The main title is non-diegetic: the characters cannot hear it.
Calling any recurring tune a leitmotif without saying what it is tied to. A leitmotif belongs to a character, place or idea.
Naming the interval wrongly. B flat up to F is a perfect fifth — count the letter names, B C D E F.
Describing the action music only as *exciting*. The devices are faster tempo, dissonance, ostinato, brass stabs and percussion.
Writing a paragraph on each section in a comparison instead of a paragraph on each element.
Using context as decoration. *1977* earns a mark only when it explains something audible, such as the revival of the full symphonic sound.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer ties every device to the job it does for the film: the brass announces a hero, the rising fifth sounds open and confident, the dissonance and ostinato make the chase relentless. It knows the facts without hesitating and uses the context only where it explains a sound — the late-Romantic orchestra as a revival of Golden Age Hollywood. In a comparison it works element by element across both sections and finishes by saying what the differences achieve: a character presented against an event depicted.
